subject: treasureChest
pitch: A pirate's treasure chest with its lid thrown open. Weathered dark wood planks bound with rusty iron straps and studs, a heavy padlock hanging loose, and spilling out of it: gold coins, a pearl necklace, a jewelled goblet and a few red and green gems. A small skull-and-crossbones is carved on the front.
reasoning:
I'm structuring this as a single TypeScript module needing a root joint for the chest and a hinge joint for the lid, then sketching rough dimensions for the chest body and lid placement with the hinge at the back.

For the lid geometry, I'm working out a low-poly half-cylinder shape using a rotated CylinderGeometry so its curved face forms the rounded top, carefully tracking how the axis rotation maps coordinates to get the correct open half facing upward.

Since the lid interior needs to be visible when opened but cylinders are single-sided, I'm planning to add an inner lining shell with a slightly smaller radius and manually reversed winding order so its normals face inward, giving it a visible interior surface.

For the body, I'm constructing it as an open box made from five separate wall pieces (floor, front, back, left, right) with thin wall thickness so the interior remains visible.

Adding wood grain texture...

Placing iron straps at symmetric x positions on both the body and the curved lid, using proud boxes and half-cylinder shells with rust mottled paint, then adding small stud spheres spaced along each strap and corner brackets at the body's edges.

I'm also designing a hanging padlock at the front staple: a small brass/iron box for the lock body paired with a partial torus shackle rotated open, swinging slightly from the hasp plate to look unlocked.

I'm placing a carved skull on the body's front face below where the lock hangs, sizing and positioning it so the two elements don't overlap.

The decal should target the painted front wall mesh, positioned to fit between the straps at x=±0.3, so placing the skull at x=-0.17 with width 0.16 keeps it clear. Now I'm thinking through the treasure pile inside the chest—a flattened, low-poly gold mound built from a scaled sphere geometry, heaped up near the rim.

Still placing coins...

I need to make sure nothing sinks more than about 2% of the total height, so I'm adjusting the sphere's vertical position and scale so its lowest point stays just above the floor, and setting the chest floor box to sit exactly at y=0.

Now I'm working out the lid's hinge rotation at the back edge, calculating how rotating roughly -110° about the x-axis moves the front of the lid upward and the top surface back, so the lid appears properly open with its dome swinging away from the viewer.

I'm checking the extreme points of the lid's arc after rotation to make sure nothing dips below ground level, tracing through the back edge and outer dome positions to verify the geometry stays consistent.

Now I'm setting up the joint hierarchy -- defining the chest as root, with lid and lock joints positioned relative to it, and marking the lid's role as a hinge for the -110 degree opening rotation. I'm working out where the lid's component parts sit relative to the joint's centered geometry.

I'm refining the hinge radius and placement so the lid curve fits flush against the body's outer wall thickness, settling on a slightly oversized radius for a small overhang. Now I'm checking how the lid's inner lining and end caps fit together, making sure the open ends line up properly with the wall thickness so there's no visible gap when viewed from inside.

Figuring out how to add inward-facing end plates so viewers inside the lid don't see through the exposed rim between the inner and outer radii. I'm working out the geometry rotations needed to orient these half-disc plates so their normals face into the lid cavity at each end.

Then I'm adding thin rim strips along the front and back edges to close the gap, applying a deep red lining paint to the interior walls matching the dark wood body. For the treasure inside, I'm placing faceted gem shapes (octahedra) in red and green scattered on the heap, plus starting work on a draped pearl necklace made from a curved string of spheres.

Mapping out the necklace path now, tracing pearls from inside the heap, over the front rim, and cascading down the outside of the chest.

For the goblet, I'm defining a lathe profile that builds a jeweled standing cup with a slim stem and flared bowl, placed tilted atop the treasure mound.

Now I'm working out where to scatter small gems around the cup rim, calculating the mound's curved surface height to seat the goblet base correctly, and tilting the whole piece about 20 degrees so it leans naturally into the pile of coins.

I'm also planning the coin heap itself, keeping each coin as a separate part but budgeting around 90 coins to stay under the overall part and triangle limits, using low-segment cylinders to keep the geometry cheap.

For colors, I'll reuse a small gold palette as shared string materials so coins can share geometry and material instances efficiently. Each coin gets a randomized tilt rotation and slight y-offset so the pile looks natural, with extra coins added spilling over the front edge of the heap.

For the wood I'm building a weathered material combining a mottled base with grain striping, then layering boundary lines to separate planks—using axis orientation differently for the lid versus the sides so the plank direction reads correctly on the cylinder top.

For iron I'm defining a rusted metal paint mixing dark iron tones with rust-orange mottling, keeping studs as plain flat colors to save texture budget.

I'm working out part placement: straps positioned along the front and sides, plus corner brackets as thin boxes placed slightly proud of the box's outer edges to sit at the corners convincingly.

Simplifying the strap layout to just a lower horizontal band across front, sides, and back, with a top band only on the sides, skipping the front's upper band since it conflicts with the lock staple. For the lid, I'm planning half-cylinder shells to form the strap shapes.

Writing half-cylinder geometry...

For the hasp, I'm placing a small curved plate at the lid's front rim, positioned where z=r cosφ is small near the opening, extending as a half-shell shape so it hangs convincingly over the front lip.

I also need a keyhole plate on the body's front center with a staple ring, and then the padlock itself should hang loosely from that staple -- I'll build its shackle as an arc of torus geometry hooked through the ring.

Checking that the arc top clears the ring hole confirms the shackle threads through correctly, so now I'm sizing the padlock body as a box positioned below the shackle, aligning its depth and offset with the shackle legs in the YZ plane.

I'm setting up the lock's material colors—brass for the body and a lighter iron tone for the shackle—and organizing the staple, lock, and body into the appropriate parts groups. Then I'm defining a joint for the lock so it can pivot open about the X axis, rotating roughly 14 degrees around the staple point.

For the rotation math, I check which direction swings the lock outward rather than into the wall, settling on a negative angle so it clears properly. Then I turn to designing the skull SVG—thinking through whether to render it as a carved dark engraving on a lighter wood base or use transparent cutouts for the eye sockets to let the wood show through.

Writing SVG code...

Finishing the teeth gaps, I'm layering the crossbones and skull with the eye holes cut via evenodd rule, confirming the coordinate flip works correctly for the texture. The decal gets a white tint since the base color is dark enough to register as colorable.

Now I'm positioning the decal on the chest's front face, checking its placement against the straps and lower band so nothing overlaps awkwardly. For the gold pile, I'm placing a coin cluster and a lump spilling out the front, plus a few coins resting on the rim, making sure the heap sphere sits properly inside the floor without clipping through the walls.

To hide the gap between the rounded heap and the box's corners, I'm adding a secondary gold box beneath it that reads as more coins filling the space. Then I'm sizing the floor and front wall panels to seal the seams cleanly.

Now I'm positioning the four wall panels so their edges meet precisely at the box corners, then setting up the lid cylinder and its inner lining along with small hinge cylinders at the back corners.

Skipping feet and straps for simplicity, I'm adding a base trim box with a dark iron-wood color, then plotting seven gem positions scattered across the coin heap, checking each falls within the ellipse boundary of the pile.

I'm computing heap height at each gem position using the elliptical falloff formula, scaling gems as small octahedrons with slight vertical offsets and random rotation, then positioning a goblet nearby while checking it doesn't overlap with the gem placements.

Still computing pearl positions...

Now I'm scattering coins on the floor in front with randomized positions, adding a flat stack and a small gold pile lump for extra visual detail, bringing the total coin count to roughly 90.

Still defining lump floor height formula and coin placement, then moving to building the chest parts with a box helper function for walls and lid, applying textures per face, and setting up the lid hinge pose and joint rotation.

Defining lathe profile points...

I'll place the gems at radius .053 around the goblet, then set up the builder scaffolding with a treasure chest module using a 2048 paint size for crisper textures, and start defining the joint hierarchy for the chest and lid.

I'm adding the lock joint, then writing part placement helpers and a triangle-flipping function to fix flipped normals on geometry, plus a half-circle disc shape for the lid cross-section before moving on to stud placement.

Placing straps and bands...

Writing coin scatter logic...

Now I'm placing the hasp plate as a partial cylinder shell covering the lid front, working out the rotation and theta start/length so the rust-colored piece wraps correctly around the lid edge.

I'm skipping the hanging tab and adding hinge cylinders at the chest sides instead, positioning them small and rotated to sit under the lid. That should complete the model, so I'll write the final answer now.
